what: ACI Worldwide makes software that moves money. Its systems process payments for banks, run the national payment infrastructure in several countries, handle bill payments for utilities and billers, and detect fraud in real time as transactions pass through.
customers: Banks and payment processors, central banks and national payment schemes, retailers, and billers such as utilities and insurers collecting payments from consumers.
money: Payment processing software for banks and the real-time payment rails of national schemes.
Payment acceptance for retailers and bill payment for utilities and other billers.
moat: Payment software sits at the centre of a bank’s operations: it clears transactions, so replacing it means risking that money stops moving. Nobody does that except under extreme pressure. ACI also runs the real-time payment infrastructure in several countries, which is about as entrenched a position as software can hold — a national payment scheme does not change vendor.
risks: Only four analysts cover the stock, so the $69.75 average target rests on very thin coverage of a $5.1B company.
Reported net income of $167.0M gives a price/earnings ratio of 31.2, high for a business growing revenue in the mid single digits.
Debt of $849.1M against $196.5M of cash is meaningful, though well covered by the cash flow.
Much of the installed base is older software that customers may eventually migrate to cloud-native alternatives.
Revenue growth is modest, from $1.4B in 2021 to $1.8B in 2025.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $358.1M on $1.8B of revenue, at about 14.1 times free cash flow, with a net margin of about 12.9%.
Payment software in a bank is replaced only under extreme pressure, because the risk of a failed migration is that payments stop.
Running the real-time payment rails of national schemes is an exceptionally entrenched position.
Real-time payments are being adopted country by country, which creates new national scheme contracts.
Fraud detection is sold alongside the payment rails and grows with transaction volumes.
watch: Recurring revenue growth and new national scheme wins. The installed base is safe; new real-time payment mandates are where growth comes from.
view: ACI occupies one of the stickiest positions in enterprise software and gets very little attention for it. Its software clears payments inside banks, which means replacing it carries the risk that money stops moving — the single outcome no bank will accept. Migrations of core payment systems are measured in years, cost enormous sums, and go wrong often enough that boards avoid them. The result is an installed base that is close to permanent, even where the software is old.

Better still, ACI runs the real-time payment infrastructure for several national schemes. A country does not change the vendor behind its instant payment rails. That is as entrenched as a software position gets, and it also creates the growth engine: real-time payments are being adopted country by country, and each new scheme is a contract that lasts decades.

The financial quality is solid rather than spectacular: a 12.9% net margin, $358 million of free cash flow on $1.8 billion of revenue, and 14.1 times free cash flow. Revenue growth from $1.4 billion to $1.8 billion over four years is mid single digits — this is not a fast-growing company, and the reported 31.2 times price/earnings ratio is a demanding multiple for that rate.

The risk worth naming is the age of the software. An entrenched legacy system is safe until a cloud-native competitor offers a bank a materially cheaper, materially better alternative and the bank decides the migration risk is finally worth taking. That is slow and it does happen. Four analysts covering a $5.1 billion company means almost nobody is tracking whether it is starting to. Recurring revenue growth and new scheme wins are the two figures; at 14 times free cash flow the price is reasonable if the base holds.
bull: New national real-time payment schemes keep arriving while an irreplaceable installed base funds it, at 14 times free cash flow.
bear: Cloud-native competitors finally persuade banks the migration risk is worth taking, growth stalls in the mid single digits, and a 31 times earnings multiple contracts.
